justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish but largely range-bound view on the underlying asset priced near 30.2. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing market price, assuming that overnight and intraday drift would be minimal absent a major catalyst. The slight upward tilt in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a gentle positive drift assumption consistent with modest risk premium and recent momentum, rather than any strong directional conviction. Essentially, I was applying a near-flat drift model with a small upward bias, which is a reasonable default in the absence of strong contrary signals.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by realized and implied volatility scaled to each time horizon. At one day, the tight band of roughly ±0.8 reflects the relatively low expected daily price movement for an asset in this price range. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, the intervals widen substantially — the one-month band spans from 27.0 to 34.0, a roughly 23% total range — because uncertainty compounds over time in a roughly square-root-of-time fashion. Liquidity conditions, the bid-ask environment, and the general macro backdrop also factored into how conservatively I set the tails, with the one-month interval deliberately kept wide to respect the many unknown developments that could emerge over that period.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in macro sentiment, an unexpected policy shift by a central bank, or a sector-specific shock could easily push the price below 27.0 at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a strong positive earnings surprise, a risk-on surge in broader markets, or a short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices well above 34.0. Even at the one-day horizon, a surprise news event — geopolitical, regulatory, or earnings-related — could blow through the 29.4–31.0 band with relative ease.

It is also worth noting that my intervals are calibrated to 90% confidence, meaning I explicitly expect roughly a one-in-ten chance of the outcome falling outside the stated range at each horizon. In practice, financial markets tend to have fatter tails than standard models imply, so the true probability of an extreme outcome is likely somewhat higher than the 10% residual I've formally assigned. Readers should treat these intervals as informed estimates rather than hard boundaries, particularly at the one-month horizon where structural uncertainty is highest.
